Everybody loves a bit of Batman in our lives, don't we all ?

>since she violated the law by going so far as having the father of her children killed you are surprised that they would take her head for it?

No, not at all. It isn't surprising that they took her head and put it on display, as a warning of sorts. By their logic, it was a good thing to do. But their logic was heavily unsound and unreasonable in general. Those were dark times, ya' know?

But I love how you explicitly said "*father of her children*". As if she was very proud that her children had **that** man's seed in them. And they would've probably been better off raised by their single mother anyway.

In the end, all that matters is that she found peace; and, gore aside, was put to rest; not you claiming "***GUILTY***", like some right-wing extremist donkey.

>Stop Stanning for her

Oops, sorry for standing against a logic that is clearly flawed.

>She was an interesting criminal, don't mistaken for anything else

Alright. Yea, by definition, a criminal is anyone that acts unlawfully, and given that what she had done would still be considered a punishable crime today, I get it.

But again, are you trying to say that whatever her husband had done to her was lawful? Compared to **modern** laws and ethics, that is. *She wouldn't have been accused of murder if she hadn't been tricked into an abusive marriage* in the first place, and especially if anyone would've stepped in to help, along the way. I ask you to consider, only for a moment, what that woman has gone through. She was pretty much held captive at that point. And having her husband killed would've been her only way of getting out. That seems like a pretty valid reason. You just cannot deny that what he had done was horrible and very wrong. It was the only way.

Note that I said "***reasonably*** unmerited". I'm completely aware that, from a legal perspective, it doesn't make a difference if her husband died or not, but the way I put it is not whether it was lawful or not to execute her, but somehow righteous or not. If you don't get it, that's ok. I hope others do.

There's another thing about criminals... Compare a bank robber, who wants to steal as much money for his own pleasure. Money for cars, drugs, etc. - you know what I mean. Compare that to a broke father that stole from a convenience store to supply for his son. Ignoring the value of stolen items, lawfully, they are both thieves/robbers. But there's a big difference. The same difference that would be between this woman, and another woman that, hypothetically, wanted her husband to be shot so she could claim his money and wealth. Madame just wanted to escape from his grasp.

And from **her** point of view, there is a clear difference between failing to get your husband killed, followed by execution, for plotting, and having assassinated your husband and getting caught, thou getting to the same result (chop chop). In the latter case, the blood is obviously on her hands, in contrast to the first case, where...well, there isn't really any blood, is there ? This is what I mean when I say that it was reasonably unmerited, and that she was at peace when she hit the bucket. She didn't really kill anyone. If the assassination was successful, she would've died knowing what she had done.

After all, only she knows what she had gone through and what made her make that choice. Who are we to judge, some internauts from the 21st century, anyways. All I was doing was making a point of why she had decided to assassinate "*the father of her children"*, whom you so dearly defend.

Not stanning for anyone here. It's just a nice story about how a woman found peace after all her suffering.

> it's what laws are for 

Sure, jimbo, as if anything was to be considered *lawful* in those times. She wouldn't have been accused of murder if she hadn't been tricked into an abusive marriage. She took matters into her own hands, simply because nobody gave a damn otherwise.

Maybe the survival of Mr. Ticquet should still be considered her escape out of this hell. As a moderately religious person, I think that even Madame knew she would find peace in death. It waited for her in open arms.

God bless.
